title: Austin Scholar #234: Highlights from my talk at Harvard
author: Austin Scholar
summary: This installment of Austin Scholar prints the full text of a talk given at the Emerging School Models conference run by Harvard's Graduate School of Education and Kennedy School, delivered by an eight-year Alpha School alumna now at Stanford and interning under Alpha's head of schools. The argument runs on a historical analogy: mechanized farming pulled a generation off the land, communities taxed themselves to build public high schools, and diploma attainment went from one in ten to more than half within a generation. AI is cast as the equivalent rupture, with the complaint that schools still prepare children for the world it is replacing. The move the talk makes is to treat AI's value as time returned rather than content delivered, citing Alpha's claim that core academics fit into two hours a day and that the recovered afternoon goes to building, performing, gardening and community contribution. Teachers are said to gain the same dividend in time per child. The talk then announces a longitudinal study with Harvard's Human Flourishing Program, framed as an attempt to submit a bold model to independent evidence. The newsletter's separate Scholar's Sources section sits behind a paid wall and is not part of this record.
points: The high school movement of the early twentieth century is used as the precedent for rebuilding school around a technological rupture rather than resisting it.
AI's contribution is framed as compression of core academics into roughly two hours, with the school day's remainder reallocated to projects, performance and service.
The talk positions itself inside an international shift from narrow academic outcomes toward flourishing, including mental and physical health, meaning and character.
A longitudinal collaboration with Harvard's Human Flourishing Program is presented as the evidence check on Alpha's own claims, including its weaknesses.
Teachers are cast as beneficiaries rather than casualties, gaining time to know and challenge individual children.
quotes: When technology transforms the world children will inherit, how should schools change to prepare them?

A century ago, tractors rolled onto American farms and began mechanizing work that had fed rural families for generations. In 1910, one in three American workers farmed; most of their children would not.

Today, we face a similar turning point. Artificial intelligence is entering every workplace, transforming what people do and what it takes to thrive. Yet our schools still prepare children for the world AI is replacing.
If AI is used well, AI can remake the school day. Every child can master academics more thoroughly, at their own pace, and in a fraction of the time.
Then we give children their time back: to learn to build a go-kart with friends, write and perform their own play, or plant a garden that helps feed their neighbors.
Alpha is an innovative model, but we want to ground it in evidence, so that what we build is not only bold, but true.
That means letting go of the school you remember. Farm families had to do the same thing when they sent their children to high schools that almost none of them had attended.
